checks.claim: Key: with each beat the heart pumps blood around the body
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the central pump of the circulatory system', propelling blood to deliver oxygen and nutrients; KidsHealth: 'With each heartbeat, the heart sends blood throughout your body'.

checks.claim: Each throb at the wrist comes from one heartbeat (pulse at the radial artery)
checks.note: Pulse results from the ejection of blood by the ventricles into the aorta, a pressure wave felt at superficial arteries; radial artery at the wrist is a common site.

checks.claim: About 80 beats a minute is a normal pulse for a boy
checks.note: 70-110 bpm for ages 6-12; 60-100 for adults. 80 is in range for either.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It makes new blood for the body' (blood is made in bone marrow)
checks.note: 'All blood cells originate from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow.' The heart makes no blood.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It cleans waste out of the blood' (kidneys and liver do)
checks.note: Kidneys filter wastes from blood; Grokipedia Blood: liver detoxifies ammonia, kidneys filter soluble wastes. The heart does not clean blood (a documented grade 3-5 misconception).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It makes energy for the body'
checks.note: Energy (ATP) is made in each cell by cellular respiration; the heart pumps, it does not make energy for the body.

checks.claim: Context: the heart is a muscle about the size of a fist
checks.note: 'a vital muscular organ'; 'roughly the size of a closed fist'; myocardium is cardiac muscle. 'A muscle' is the standard child-level wording (LibreTexts, KidsHealth 'heart muscle').

checks.claim: Context: blood made in the marrow inside bones, other organs clean waste out of it
checks.note: Bone marrow; kidneys and liver.

checks.claim: Key: blood brings oxygen and food (nutrients) to each part of the body
checks.note: 'delivering oxygen and nutrients to cells while removing metabolic waste products such as carbon dioxide'; KidsHealth heart page says the same.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It carries air from the nose to the lungs'
checks.note: Air reaches the lungs through the airway: nose/mouth, trachea (windpipe), bronchi. Blood carries dissolved oxygen from the lungs, not air from the nose.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It breaks down food into tiny pieces'
checks.note: Digestion (mouth, stomach, small intestine) breaks food down; blood carries the absorbed products.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It carries signals along the nerves'
checks.note: Nerves carry nerve signals. Blood does carry hormones (chemical messages), but not 'along the nerves', so the choice stays wrong as worded.

checks.claim: Context: blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and digested food in the small intestine; carries away carbon dioxide
checks.note: O2 loading in the lungs; absorbed substances from the gastrointestinal tract via the portal vein. (Fats go first into lymph, a detail below grade level; the simplification holds for most digested food.)

checks.claim: Context: air down the windpipe, food broken down in stomach and intestines, signals along nerves
checks.note: Consistent with KidsHealth lungs and digestive pages.

checks.claim: Key: cells break down food with oxygen for energy, leaving carbon dioxide, carried by blood to the lungs and breathed out
checks.note: Aerobic respiration produces 'ATP, carbon dioxide, and water'. KidsHealth lungs: 'As cells do their jobs, they make and give off carbon dioxide'; 'Blood rich in carbon dioxide travels to the heart, which pumps it to the lungs'.

checks.claim: Wrong: Carbon monoxide
checks.note: The body does make a trace of CO (about 450 micromol a day) and some is breathed out, but it comes from breaking down heme, not from cells breaking down food for energy, which the stem specifies. Fair wrong choice.

checks.claim: Wrong: Oxygen
checks.note: Oxygen is used up (21% in, about 16% out); it is not the waste gas.

checks.claim: Wrong: Nitrogen
checks.note: Nitrogen about 78% in and about 78% out; not made by cells.

checks.claim: Context: nitrogen makes up most of the air and comes back out in about the same amount
checks.note: Exhaled nitrogen approximately 78%.

checks.claim: Context: carbon monoxide is a poison given off when fuel burns badly in stoves, fires and engines
checks.note: 'incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels'; furnaces, stoves, fireplaces, generators, vehicles; toxic through its affinity for hemoglobin.

checks.claim: Key: the stomach, a stretchy muscular organ where acid juices soak food and the walls churn it into a thick soup
checks.note: 'a J-shaped, hollow, muscular organ'; rugae 'allow expansion'; parietal cells make hydrochloric acid (pH about 1-3.5); 'mechanical digestion via churning motions'; chyme 'a viscous, semi-liquid mixture'. KidsHealth: 'The stomach muscles churn and mix the food with digestive juices that have acids and enzymes'.

checks.claim: Food reaches it down a tube (the esophagus)
checks.note: Peristalsis forces food 'down through the esophagus to the stomach'.

checks.claim: Wrong: the small intestine
checks.note: Not fed by the swallowing tube; pancreatic bicarbonate neutralizes the acid chyme, pH 6-7 in the duodenum, so it is not where strong acid soaks the food.

checks.claim: Wrong: the large intestine
checks.note: Receives undigested material from the small intestine and absorbs water; no acid soak.

checks.claim: Wrong: the liver
checks.note: Food never passes through the liver; it makes bile and processes nutrients in the blood.

checks.claim: Context: soup moves on to the small intestine
checks.note: Chyme released through the pyloric sphincter into the duodenum.

checks.claim: Key: most digested food passes into the blood in the small intestine
checks.note: Absorbs 'over 90% of nutrients and water', through villi into the bloodstream or lymphatics. KidsHealth: 'The villi are the vehicles through which nutrients can be absorbed into the blood'. Fats go first into lymph (lacteals) and reach the blood later; 'most' keeps the key true.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It is soaked in strong acid'
checks.note: Bicarbonate neutralizes the stomach's acid chyme; pH 6-7 in the duodenum.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It is made into solid waste'
checks.note: Only the undigested leftover goes on to the large intestine, which forms feces.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It is stored until it is needed'
checks.note: The stomach, not the small intestine, is the temporary food reservoir; the stem's 'there' rules out later storage in liver or fat.

checks.claim: Context: villi are tiny finger-like bumps; food passes through them into the blood; the large intestine takes out water and forms solid waste
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'finger-like villi'; KidsHealth: large intestine's 'main job is to remove water from the undigested matter and form solid waste'.

checks.claim: Stem: the small intestine is a long tube coiled up inside the belly
checks.note: 'a long, coiled tubular structure', about 3-5 m in living people (no number given in the question).

checks.claim: Key: nerves carry messages between brain and muscles/senses
checks.note: 'a cordlike organ... composed of multiple bundles of axons'; sensory nerves carry impulses toward the CNS, motor nerves away to muscles; up to 120 m/s ('in a flash').

checks.claim: Stem: the brain is the body's control centre
checks.note: 'serves as the body's command center, processing sensory input, coordinating voluntary movements'.

checks.claim: Wrong: veins (carry blood back to the heart)
checks.note: 'veins carry blood back to the heart'.

checks.claim: Wrong: tendons (tie muscles to bones)
checks.note: 'Skeletal muscle is attached by cord-like tendons to bone'.

checks.claim: Wrong: ligaments (tie bones to bones)
checks.note: Bones fastened to other bones by 'long, fibrous straps called ligaments'.

checks.claim: Context: nerves are thread-like bundles branching from brain and spinal cord to every part of the body
checks.note: KidsHealth: the spinal cord 'contains threadlike nerves that branch out to every organ and body part'; Grokipedia Nerve: signals between the CNS and peripheral tissues.

checks.claim: Key: the skull guards the brain
checks.note: 'The skull is the skeletal structure of the head that encloses and protects the brain.' KidsHealth: 'The skull protects the brain'.

checks.claim: Stem: bones hold the body up, give it shape, and some protect soft organs
checks.note: 'Bones provide support for our bodies and help form our shape'.

checks.claim: Wrong: the ribs (cage around heart and lungs)
checks.note: 'The ribs form a cage that shelters the heart and lungs.' Not the brain.

checks.claim: Wrong: the spine (guards the spinal cord)
checks.note: The spinal cord 'is protected by the backbone, or spinal column'; the brain (brainstem included) sits inside the skull, so the spine does not guard the brain.

checks.claim: Wrong: the pelvis
checks.note: Shelters the bladder and part of the gut; far from the brain.

checks.claim: Context: the skull is 22 bones joined together
checks.note: 'The human skull comprises 22 bones in adults, with 21 forming immovable joints and the mandible being mobile', joined by fibrous sutures (ear ossicles excluded). The movable jaw is still joined at a joint, so 'joined together' holds.

checks.claim: Context: the spine guards the spinal cord, the pathway for messages between the brain and the body
checks.note: Matches KidsHealth wording.

checks.claim: Key: a muscle moves a bone by pulling on it
checks.note: Macmillan (Morris, Biology): 'Muscles can generate force only by pulling, not pushing, on the skeleton'; KidsHealth: 'Muscles can pull bones, but they can't push them'.

checks.claim: Stem: the biceps is at the front of the upper arm and bends the elbow, raising the hand toward the shoulder
checks.note: 'situated in the anterior compartment of the upper arm'; a flexor of the elbow (Grokipedia calls it a synergist of the brachialis, the main flexor; 'when it works, the elbow bends' is still true). Macmillan: flexors (the biceps) 'contract to bring the arm toward the shoulder'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'By pushing on it'
checks.note: Muscles cannot push; 'muscles can push and pull' is a listed misconception.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'By pumping blood into it'
checks.note: The heart is the pump; muscles move bones by contraction.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'By sending a signal to it'
checks.note: Motor nerves send signals to muscles; muscles do not move bones by signalling them.

checks.claim: Context: a working muscle gets shorter and pulls on the bone through a tendon
checks.note: KidsHealth: muscles 'contract (shorten or tighten)'; Grokipedia Tendon/Biceps: inserts by its tendon. True for the stem's case (the biceps lifting the hand). Strictly, a muscle can also work without shortening (isometric) or while lengthening (eccentric, e.g. lowering a load) per Grokipedia Muscle_contraction; optional tweak for full safety: 'A working muscle tightens and gets shorter, pulling on the bone...' or 'To move a bone, a muscle gets shorter...'.

checks.claim: Context: muscles pull but never push, so they work in pairs; the triceps at the back straightens the elbow
checks.note: 'the antagonist triceps brachii, which extends the elbow'; KidsHealth: muscles 'work in pairs of flexors and extensors'.

checks.claim: Context: nerves carry the signal; the heart does the pumping
checks.note: Motor nerves transmit impulses to muscles.

checks.claim: Key: the skin is the largest organ in the human body; is 'largest in the human body' safe given the liver is the largest internal organ?
checks.note: Guinness uses almost the same words: 'Skin is the largest organ in a human body', and calls the liver 'his largest internal organ'. Grokipedia Skin: 'the body's largest organ'; KidsHealth and MedlinePlus agree; Healthline, CDC, Britannica Kids all qualify the liver as largest INTERNAL (or solid) organ. The stem does not say 'inside', so it is safe. (The 2018 proposal that the interstitium is an organ, perhaps the largest, is not established and it is not a choice.) Optional extra safety: 'the largest organ of the human body'.

checks.claim: Wrong: the liver
checks.note: 'the largest solid organ'; 1.4 kg (women) to 1.8 kg (men); lighter than the skin in every source found.

checks.claim: Wrong: the brain
checks.note: About 1.4 kg.

checks.claim: Wrong: the stomach
checks.note: A hollow J-shaped organ, far lighter than skin or liver.

checks.claim: Context: an adult's skin weighs nearly 4 kg, more than twice the liver
checks.note: Guinness: skin 'weighs about 3.8 kg' (for a 70 kg man), liver 'only about 1.5 kg': 2.5 times. Other sources vary: Bananas-for-Scale/BiologyInsights 3-4 kg; MedlinePlus 'about 6 pounds' (2.7 kg, which against a 1.4-1.8 kg liver is closer to 'about twice'); up to about 15% of body weight if the fat layer is counted (Live Science). The figure is Guinness's and the direction (skin much heavier) holds in every source. Optional softer wording: 'about 4 kilograms, roughly twice as much as the liver'.

checks.claim: Context: the liver is the largest organ inside the body
checks.note: Guinness, CDC, Cleveland Clinic: largest internal organ.

checks.claim: Context: skin covers and protects the whole body, keeps germs out and water in, feels heat, cold and touch
checks.note: 'a dynamic barrier that protects against pathogens, physical injury, ultraviolet radiation, and water loss'; 'Sensory receptors in the dermis detect touch, pressure, pain, and temperature'.

unit_notes: All 9 questions check out. Lead's specific questions: (1) Skin as largest organ: the stem 'largest in the human body' matches Guinness's own wording; the liver is consistently qualified as largest INTERNAL/solid organ, so the key is safe. The context's 'nearly 4 kg, more than twice the liver' is Guinness's model adult; MedlinePlus gives 6 lb (2.7 kg), so 'roughly twice' would be safer but the current line is sourced. (2) Muscles pull, never push: textbook-standard (Macmillan Biology, KidsHealth). The context's 'A working muscle gets shorter' is true for the stem's lifting case but not for every kind of muscle work (isometric, eccentric); optional reword. (3) Small intestine: the stomach does absorb a little (alcohol, aspirin, some water), but no wrong choice in that question says the stomach or claims absorption elsewhere; 'soaked in strong acid' is wrong because bicarbonate neutralizes the chyme (pH 6-7); 'stored until needed' is wrong because 'there' fixes the place, and the small intestine is not the food reservoir (the stomach is). (4) Carbon monoxide: the body makes a trace (about 450 micromol/day) from heme breakdown and some is exhaled, but the stem ties the gas to cells breaking down food for energy, which CO is not, so the choice is fair. (5) Heart and blood: pump, fist size, 60-100 bpm adult / 70-110 bpm ages 6-12 (80 fits), marrow makes blood cells, kidneys/liver clean it, arteries out / veins back: all confirmed. Fats enter lymph before blood, below grade level; 'most digested food' keeps both blood claims true.
